questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. Who establishes risk appetite
questions.question: The founders of a new digital bank in Indonesia ask internal auditor Dewi Santoso who should establish how much credit risk the bank is willing to take. Which party is the BEST answer?

options.A: The bank's senior management
options.B: The bank's board of directors
options.C: The bank's risk management function
options.D: The bank's internal audit function

questions.key_concept: The board establishes the organization's risk appetite; senior management proposes it and manages within it; internal audit assesses.
questions.pre_read: Separate three verbs: who establishes, who proposes and operates, and who assesses.
questions.correct_explanation: Establishing risk appetite is a governance decision, so it belongs to the board. Both of The IIA's 2026 Statements of Position, on enterprise risk management and on the Three Lines Model, give the board that role. Senior management is the closest choice because it usually proposes the appetite and must run the bank inside it, but proposing a limit and working within it is different from establishing it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: senior management usually drafts the appetite and manages within it, but it answers to the board, which establishes how much risk the bank will take.
wrong_explanations.C: The risk management function is a second-line role that supports, monitors and challenges. It measures risk against the appetite; it does not establish it.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives assurance and advice on how appetite is established and used. Establishing it is a governance decision, which internal audit does not take.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a risk function supports and monitors within limits set above it, and D, because internal audit assures and advises and takes no governance decisions.
Final two: B beats A because management proposes the appetite and operates within it, while establishing it is the board's governance role.
Exam cue: when a question asks who establishes risk appetite or sets direction, look to the board; management proposes and runs, and internal audit assesses.

questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. Independent assurance over a second-line function
questions.question: At a Finnish insurer, the board wants independent assurance for itself that the risk management function's monitoring of underwriting limits works. Which party is BEST placed to provide it?

options.A: The external audit firm
options.B: The compliance function
options.C: The underwriting management team
options.D: The internal audit function

questions.key_concept: Internal audit, the third line, gives the board independent assurance, including over second-line functions; external auditors serve outside stakeholders.
questions.pre_read: Ask who each party works for and who sets the limits of its work.
questions.correct_explanation: The internal audit function is the third line: it gives the board independent, objective assurance over governance, risk management and control, including over second-line functions such as risk management (The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model). The external audit firm is independent too, but it serves stakeholders outside the insurer, and law or regulation sets its scope, usually the financial statements. It does not replace internal assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the external audit firm is independent, but it serves outside stakeholders and its scope is set by law, usually the financial statements, not this monitoring.
wrong_explanations.B: Compliance is itself a second-line function inside management. It supports and challenges, but it lacks the independence from management that the board is asking for.
wrong_explanations.C: Underwriting managers are the first line and own the limits being monitored. Their own review is useful management information, not independent assurance.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a second-line function sits inside management, and C, because first-line managers own the very limits being monitored.
Final two: D beats A because internal audit's assurance is for the board and covers the second line, while the external firm serves outside stakeholders within a scope set by law.
Exam cue: when the board wants independent assurance for itself over management or a second-line function, think third line: the internal audit function.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. Evidence of culture in practice
questions.question: Internal auditor Karim Benali is assessing how a Moroccan retailer promotes an ethical culture. Which evidence would tell Karim MOST about the culture in practice?

options.A: How managers treated staff who had raised a concern
options.B: Signed staff acknowledgments of the code of conduct
options.C: The board minute that approved the code of conduct
options.D: The length and detail of the written ethics policies

questions.key_concept: Culture is judged by behavior and its consequences, not by the existence of written policies.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask whether it shows what people do or only what was written down.
questions.correct_explanation: Culture shows in what people do and in what leaders reward or punish, so the treatment of staff who spoke up is direct evidence of it. Standard 9.1 has the chief audit executive consider how the organization promotes an ethical culture, and Standard 1.2's considerations treat policies as only part of that culture's basis. Signed acknowledgments, the closest choice, show that staff received the code, not that anyone follows it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a signature shows that staff received and read the code. It says nothing about whether people follow it or what happens when they do not.
wrong_explanations.C: Board approval shows the code exists and has formal backing. Written intent at the top is different from the behavior leaders model and reward.
wrong_explanations.D: Longer, more detailed policies show effort in writing. A thick manual can sit beside a culture that rewards cutting around it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because approving a code shows intent on paper, and D, because longer policies show effort in writing, not how people behave.
Final two: A beats B because a signature shows the code was received, while the treatment of people who speak up shows what leaders actually reward.
Exam cue: for culture or tone at the top, prefer evidence of behavior and consequences over evidence that a document exists.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. Engagement-level risk assessment
questions.question: Planning a first engagement on vessel maintenance at a Philippine ferry operator, internal auditor Luz Reyes finds one line on it in the organization-wide risk assessment. Which approach BEST meets the Standards?

options.A: Adopt that line as the engagement risk assessment
options.B: Rely on the maintenance manager's own list of key risks
options.C: Understand the activity, then identify and rank its key risks
options.D: Start control testing and record risks as they come up

questions.key_concept: Each engagement needs its own risk assessment: understand the activity, identify significant risks, consider fraud, and rank them.
questions.pre_read: Decide which sources are inputs to the internal auditor's work and which is the work itself.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires internal auditors to understand the activity under review, find the risks that could matter most to its objectives, consider fraud and put the risks in order for review. The assessment behind the internal audit plan is one input. So is the manager's list, which makes it the closest choice, but internal auditors must form their own view, and a manager may leave out risks such as fraud.

wrong_explanations.A: The organization-wide assessment supports the internal audit plan and is broad. It is an input to engagement planning, not the engagement's own risk assessment.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: management's view of its risks is valuable input, but the internal auditor must form an independent view, including fraud risks a manager may not list.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing follows planning. Without an assessment of the activity's risks there is no basis for objectives, scope or a work program.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the plan-level assessment is only an input, and D, because risks are assessed before objectives, scope and tests are set.
Final two: C beats B because management's list informs the assessment, while the internal auditor must still understand the activity and judge its risks independently.
Exam cue: at the start of an engagement, look for understanding the activity and assessing its own risks; other assessments are inputs, not substitutes.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. A weak decision process with a good outcome
questions.question: A Peruvian transit agency's charter requires a risk analysis before any fare change, but internal auditor Rosa Quispe finds the last change was approved without one, and revenue rose. What is Rosa's BEST course?

options.A: Report the skipped risk analysis as a governance finding
options.B: Hold the point unless a later fare change loses revenue
options.C: Conclude the approval process works, given the revenue gain
options.D: Review each future fare change before the committee approves it

questions.key_concept: A gap between criteria and condition is a finding whatever the outcome; a good result can hide a weak decision process.
questions.pre_read: Name the criterion and the condition before you look at how things turned out.
questions.correct_explanation: The charter is the criterion and the skipped analysis is the condition, so there is a gap to evaluate and report whatever the result. Standard 14.2 requires a difference between criteria and condition to be noted and evaluated, and Standard 14.3 judges significance by likelihood and impact, not by whether harm has happened yet. Waiting for a loss, the closest choice, lets a known weakness in decision-making run on.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it keeps the point alive, but significance rests on likelihood and impact, so the gap is reportable now, before a decision made this way goes wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: One good outcome does not test the process. A decision taken with no risk analysis can succeed by luck and fail the next time.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviewing each decision before approval would make internal audit part of management's control, and it could not then assess that control objectively.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a good outcome can come from a weak decision process, and D, because reviewing each decision beforehand makes internal audit part of the control.
Final two: A beats B because a gap from the criteria is a finding now; its significance depends on likelihood and impact, not on a loss having occurred.
Exam cue: when the outcome was fine but a required step was skipped, judge the process against its criteria, not the result.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. A breach of the organization's own policy
questions.question: An Irish retailer's published refund policy promises refunds within 7 days, the law allows 30, and internal auditor Aoife Byrne finds refunds take about 20 days. How should Aoife BEST classify this?

options.A: A breach of consumer law to report to the regulator
options.B: A fraud indicator to refer for investigation
options.C: An acceptable result, as refunds are inside the legal limit
options.D: A compliance gap against the retailer's own policy

questions.key_concept: Compliance covers the organization's own policies and commitments as well as law; the law is the minimum.
questions.pre_read: List every rule in the facts that binds the retailer, then compare each with what happens.
questions.correct_explanation: Compliance, as the Standards' glossary uses the word, reaches every binding rule: law, regulation, contract and the organization's own policies and procedures. The retailer's published policy is therefore a criterion, and 20 days against a 7-day promise is a gap to report. Meeting the 30-day legal limit, the closest choice, only shows that the law is satisfied. The law is the minimum, and the retailer has set itself a stricter rule.

wrong_explanations.A: No law is broken: refunds arrive inside the 30 days the law allows. The requirement that is missed is the retailer's own 7-day policy.
wrong_explanations.B: Fraud involves intent and deceit. Slow refunds point to a process that misses its own standard, with nothing here suggesting deliberate dishonesty.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the law is met, but compliance also means keeping the organization's own policies, and this one promises customers 7 days.

tips: Eliminate: A, because refunds arrive within the 30 days the law allows, and B, because nothing in the facts points to intent or deceit.
Final two: D beats C because meeting the law is the minimum; compliance also covers the policies an organization sets for itself.
Exam cue: when conduct is legal but breaks the organization's own policy, contract or code, it is still a compliance gap to report.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. An ethics concern outside the engagement scope
questions.question: During a stock count engagement at a Nigerian drug distributor, internal auditor Chidi Okafor learns that a purchasing manager, outside the engagement scope, took costly supplier gifts against policy. What is Chidi's BEST course?

options.A: Note it for the next purchasing engagement in the plan
options.B: Report it as the organization's policies require
options.C: Take no action on a matter outside the approved scope
options.D: Tell the supplier to stop sending gifts to the distributor's staff

questions.key_concept: Behavior against the organization's ethical expectations must be reported under its policies, whether or not it falls inside the engagement scope.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the duty in play belongs to this engagement or to every internal auditor at all times.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 1.2, an internal auditor who comes across conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations must report it in the way its policies and procedures lay down. The duty does not depend on the engagement's scope. Saving the point for a later purchasing engagement, the closest choice, treats an ethics breach as a planning input and keeps it from the people with authority to act on it now.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the matter may well shape a later engagement, but an ethics breach must be reported now through the set channel, not parked as a planning note.
wrong_explanations.C: Scope limits what the engagement tests. It does not limit the duty to report conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations.
wrong_explanations.D: Dealing with the supplier is management's decision. The internal auditor reports the concern inside the organization through the channel its policies set.

tips: Eliminate: C, because scope limits testing and not the duty to report, and D, because dealing with the supplier is management's decision.
Final two: B beats A because an ethics breach is reported when found, through the channel policy sets; a planning note delays those who can act.
Exam cue: when an internal auditor finds unethical conduct outside the scope, the answer is still to report it through the organization's set channel.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. Risk with a possible upside
questions.question: At a risk workshop for a Portuguese solar developer, the facilitator drops 'subsidy may be extended' from the register as good news. Which treatment should internal auditor Inês Duarte consider MOST appropriate?

options.A: Leave it out until the subsidy decision is certain
options.B: Record it if it could also cause a loss
options.C: Record it as a risk with a possible upside
options.D: Leave it out of a register meant for threats

questions.key_concept: Risk is what uncertainty may do to objectives, for better or worse, so opportunities belong in the risk picture.
questions.pre_read: Test the item against two questions: is the outcome uncertain, and would it affect an objective?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary treats risk as what uncertainty may do to objectives, for better or for worse, and The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management speaks of threats and opportunities. A possible subsidy extension is uncertain and bears on the developer's objectives, so it belongs in the register. Recording it only if it could also cause a loss, the closest choice, still treats risk as downside alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Once the decision is certain there is no uncertainty left to manage. Risk identification deals with events that may or may not happen.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it keeps the item in view, but it makes a possible loss the test, and risk covers favorable effects on objectives as well.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk is wider than threats. Uncertainty that could help an objective is part of risk, so the register is the place for it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because risk is about events that are still uncertain, and D, because risk covers opportunities as well as threats.
Final two: C beats B because an uncertain event that could help an objective is a risk in its own right, with no loss needed.
Exam cue: when an option treats risk as harm alone, check the definition: uncertainty can help or hurt an objective.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. Residual risk and controls not yet in place
questions.question: A Sri Lankan toll-road operator's register rates cash-theft risk 'low residual', counting cameras approved for installation next year. Which conclusion by internal auditor Nimal Perera is MOST accurate?

options.A: Residual risk is understated until the cameras are actually working
options.B: Residual risk is fairly rated because the cameras are funded
options.C: Inherent risk is overstated because cameras will reduce it
options.D: Residual risk should be rated by internal audit instead

questions.key_concept: Residual risk is what remains after the management actions already implemented; planned controls do not reduce it yet.
questions.pre_read: Check the timing of each management action against the date of the rating.
questions.correct_explanation: In the Standards' glossary, residual risk is what is left of inherent risk once management's actions have been implemented. Cameras that are approved but not installed stop no theft today, so the register shows less risk than the operator carries. Approved funding, the closest choice, shows intent and a plan; it changes the rating only when the control is in place and working.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: funding shows commitment, but residual risk counts only actions already implemented. Until the cameras work, the exposure is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.C: Inherent risk is rated before any management action, so controls, present or future, do not change it. The cameras bear on residual risk only.
wrong_explanations.D: Management owns the register and its ratings. The internal auditor assesses whether a rating is supported and reports the gap for management to correct.

tips: Eliminate: C, because inherent risk is rated before any controls, and D, because management owns the register and its ratings.
Final two: A beats B because residual risk reflects actions already implemented; approval and funding do not lower the exposure until the control works.
Exam cue: when a residual rating counts a control that is planned, approved or recommended but not in place, the rating is too low.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. Recognizing a risk tolerance statement
questions.question: Internal auditor Hana Sato reads four statements in the board papers of a Japanese ambulance service. Which one BEST expresses a risk tolerance?

options.A: We accept very little risk to patient safety
options.B: Late-response risk is rated high before any controls
options.C: Vehicle breakdown losses are covered by fleet insurance
options.D: Reach 90% of calls in 8 minutes, with 85% the floor

questions.key_concept: Risk appetite is the kind and amount of risk taken overall; risk tolerance is the acceptable variation in performance around an objective.
questions.pre_read: Look for the statement that ties a measurable band to one objective.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation in performance around an objective, so it reads as a target with a band: 90 percent, and no lower than 85. The patient-safety statement is the closest choice, but it describes risk appetite: the kind and amount of risk the service is willing to take overall, with no measure attached. Both terms are defined in the Standards' glossary.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it states how much risk the service will take overall, with no measure. That is risk appetite, the broader of the two terms.
wrong_explanations.B: A rating made before controls describes inherent risk. It says how large the exposure is, not how much variation in results is acceptable.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance is a risk response: it shares part of a loss with another party. It sets no acceptable range for performance.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a rating before controls is inherent risk, and C, because insurance is a response that shares a loss.
Final two: D beats A because tolerance is a measurable band around one objective, while the safety statement is the broad appetite.
Exam cue: a broad statement of how much risk to take is appetite; a target with an acceptable range of results is tolerance.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. Finding the weak element of the cycle
questions.question: An Egyptian cement maker's monthly risk indicators correctly flagged three limit breaches, but nobody told senior management or the board. Which part of the risk cycle should the internal auditor report as the MAIN weakness?

options.A: Monitoring whether risks and their responses are changing
options.B: Assessing the likelihood and impact of each identified risk
options.C: Reporting significant risks to those who oversee
options.D: Identifying the risks that threaten the firm's objectives

questions.key_concept: The risk management cycle is identify, assess, manage, monitor and report; monitoring that catches a breach still fails if nothing is escalated.
questions.pre_read: Find the last step in the facts that worked, then look at the step after it.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management names five elements: identify, assess, manage, monitor and report. Here the indicators caught the breaches accurately and on time, so monitoring did its job. What failed was the next element: significant risks were not escalated to senior management and the board, who cannot oversee what they never see. Monitoring is the closest choice because the two elements sit side by side.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: monitoring is the neighboring element, but the indicators flagged the breaches correctly, so monitoring worked. The failure came after it.
wrong_explanations.B: Nothing in the facts questions how the risks were rated. Limits and indicators exist, which suggests assessment was done.
wrong_explanations.D: The risks were known well enough to have limits and indicators. Identification is not where this process broke down.

tips: Eliminate: B, because nothing in the facts questions the ratings, and D, because risks with limits and indicators were already identified.
Final two: C beats A because the indicators flagged the breaches correctly, so monitoring worked; the escalation that should follow never happened.
Exam cue: place each fact in the cycle of identify, assess, manage, monitor and report; the weakness is the first element that failed.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. Judging an accepted risk
questions.question: A Czech museum's management formally accepts minor gift-shop stock losses that sit within the board's risk appetite and cost less than extra controls would. Which conclusion by internal auditor Petra Novák is MOST reasonable?

options.A: The acceptance should be escalated to the board as unresolved
options.B: The acceptance is a legitimate response to a risk this size
options.C: Management should add controls until the losses stop
options.D: Internal audit should choose a stronger response for management

questions.key_concept: Accepting a risk within appetite is a legitimate response; only acceptance above risk appetite or risk tolerance triggers escalation.
questions.pre_read: Compare the accepted risk with the organization's own yardstick, then with the cost of treating it.
questions.correct_explanation: Accepting a risk is a valid response when the exposure sits within the organization's risk appetite and treating it would cost more than bearing it. Standard 11.5 has the chief audit executive raise an accepted risk with senior management, and then the board, only when it exceeds risk appetite or risk tolerance. Escalation, the closest choice, has no trigger here: the decision is recorded, within appetite and sensible on cost.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: escalation is right when accepted risk exceeds risk appetite or risk tolerance. Here the loss is within appetite, so nothing is unresolved.
wrong_explanations.C: Risk management aims to keep risk within appetite, not to remove it. Controls that cost more than the loss waste resources.
wrong_explanations.D: Choosing the response is management's decision. Internal audit assesses whether the response is adequate and reports its view.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the aim is risk within appetite and not zero loss, and D, because management chooses the risk response.
Final two: B beats A because escalation is triggered by risk accepted above appetite or tolerance, and this loss sits within the board's appetite.
Exam cue: an accepted risk is a concern only when it exceeds the organization's appetite or tolerance; otherwise acceptance is a valid response.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. Relying on management's risk register
questions.question: A Thai hotel group gives chief audit executive Anong Suksai a detailed management risk register. As leading practice, what should Anong do FIRST before relying on it for the internal audit plan?

options.A: Confirm that senior management has signed off the register
options.B: Use it as it stands, since management owns the risks
options.C: Set it aside and assess risks without management's input
options.D: Conclude whether the risk processes behind it are effective

questions.key_concept: Judge the process before trusting its output: management's risk register is reliable only if the risk management processes behind it work.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes any output trustworthy before you use it.
questions.correct_explanation: A register is only as good as the process that produces it. Standard 9.4's considerations say internal audit should lean on management's risk information only once it has concluded that the processes producing it work: leading practice, not a requirement. Senior management's sign-off, the closest choice, shows who answers for the register, not whether every unit contributes or ratings are kept current.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: sign-off shows ownership and accountability. It does not show that the process behind the register is complete, consistent and kept up to date.
wrong_explanations.B: Management does own the risks, but ownership does not make its register reliable. Internal audit first judges the process that produced it.
wrong_explanations.C: The plan's risk assessment must take input from the board and senior management. Management's risk information is an input to weigh, not to shut out.

tips: Eliminate: B, because owning the risks does not make the register reliable, and C, because the plan's risk assessment needs management's input.
Final two: D beats A because a signature shows who answers for the register, while reliance depends on whether the process producing it is effective.
Exam cue: before leaning on anyone's output, such as a risk register, expect the internal auditor to judge the process that produced it.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. Advisory help with a risk program
questions.question: The chief operating officer of a Tanzanian agribusiness asks the internal audit function to help with a new risk program. Which request is MOST suitable for it to accept as advisory work?

options.A: Facilitate the workshop where managers identify their risks
options.B: Keep the risk register up to date between workshops
options.C: Rank the risk responses that management should fund first
options.D: Approve each unit's risk response plan before the board sees it

questions.key_concept: Internal audit may facilitate, advise and challenge in risk management; it must not operate the process or select, rank or approve risk responses.
questions.pre_read: For each request, ask who would end up deciding or running something that management should own.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management lists facilitating risk workshops among advisory services: internal audit guides the discussion and managers reach their own conclusions. Keeping the register current, the closest choice, sounds clerical, but it means operating part of the risk process between workshops, which is management's work and would later be audited by the function that ran it. Ranking or approving responses is management decision-making.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it looks like routine support, but maintaining the register is operating the risk process, which is management's work and impairs later assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Deciding which responses get funded first is prioritizing risk responses. That is a management decision internal audit must not take.
wrong_explanations.D: Approving response plans is a management decision and makes internal audit accountable for them. Internal audit can give assurance on them instead.

tips: Eliminate: C, because ranking responses for funding is management's decision, and D, because approving plans makes internal audit accountable for them.
Final two: A beats B because facilitating leaves every conclusion with managers, while keeping the register means operating part of management's risk process.
Exam cue: in risk management, internal audit may facilitate, advise, challenge and assure; options where it operates, ranks, selects or approves are wrong.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A control linked to no risk
questions.question: In a payroll engagement at a Uruguayan school district, internal auditor Mateo Silva finds a weekly sign-off that neither staff nor documents can link to any risk. What is Mateo's BEST course?

options.A: Recommend keeping it as an extra layer of control
options.B: Delete the sign-off from the payroll procedure during fieldwork
options.C: Ask management which risk the sign-off is meant to manage
options.D: Leave it out of the results, which cover control gaps

questions.key_concept: A control exists to manage a risk to an objective; one that manages no risk is cost, and management decides what to do with it.
questions.pre_read: Start from what a control is for, then ask who can say what this one is for.
questions.correct_explanation: In the Standards' glossary a control is an action taken to manage risk and make objectives more reachable, so a sign-off tied to no risk may be pure cost. The internal auditor first works with management to learn what it is for, then judges whether it is worth reporting. Leaving it out, the closest choice, assumes results cover only gaps; Standard 14.2's considerations count chances to improve efficiency among potential findings.

wrong_explanations.A: More control is not always better control. A step that manages no risk adds cost and delay without making any objective more reachable.
wrong_explanations.B: Changing a procedure is management's action. The internal auditor raises the point and discusses it; management decides and makes any change.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: no gap is proven yet, but potential findings include chances to improve efficiency, and the purpose of the step is still unknown.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a control must serve a risk to be worth keeping, and B, because changing a procedure is management's action.
Final two: C beats D because results can include efficiency improvements, and management must first say what the sign-off is for.
Exam cue: tie every control to a risk and an objective; where no link is found, the internal auditor asks management and then reports.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. Choosing a preventive control
questions.question: A Singapore hospital pharmacy finds controlled-drug losses through a weekly count, and management asks internal auditor Wei Ling Tan for options. Which added control would BEST stop a loss before it happens?

options.A: A daily count in place of the weekly count
options.B: A locked cabinet that only named pharmacists can open
options.C: An insurance policy covering losses of controlled drugs
options.D: A monthly review of count differences by internal audit

questions.key_concept: A preventive control acts before the event; a detective control reveals it afterward, however often it runs.
questions.pre_read: Sort each option by when it acts: before the loss, or after it.
questions.correct_explanation: A control that stops the event beforehand is preventive; one that reveals it afterward is detective. Standard 13.2's considerations name both types without defining them, so the plain meaning applies. Restricting who can open the cabinet acts before any drug leaves. A daily count, the closest choice, finds a loss sooner, but still after it has happened: more frequent detection is not prevention. Management chooses which control to adopt.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: counting daily shortens the time to discovery, but a count still acts after the loss. Frequency does not turn detection into prevention.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance shares the financial loss after the event. The drugs can still go missing, so nothing is prevented.
wrong_explanations.D: A review of differences acts after the loss, and operating a control is management's job, not internal audit's.

tips: Eliminate: C, because insurance shares a loss that has already happened, and D, because internal audit does not operate management's controls.
Final two: B beats A because restricted access acts before a loss, while any count, however frequent, finds it afterward.
Exam cue: classify a control by when it acts; counts, reconciliations and reviews detect, while approvals, locks and system blocks prevent.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A recommendation that fits cause and cost
questions.question: Internal auditor Aigerim Bekova finds duplicate supplier payments of about $3,000 a year at a Kazakh rail operator, caused by duplicate supplier records. Which recommendation is BEST to discuss with management?

options.A: A system rule that blocks a second record per supplier
options.B: A second manual review of every supplier payment before release
options.C: A quarterly recovery review by an outside firm
options.D: A cleanup of the supplier records by internal audit

questions.key_concept: A fitting recommendation addresses the root cause and costs less than the harm it prevents; management decides and implements.
questions.pre_read: Find the cause stated in the facts, then weigh what each option would cost against the loss.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.4 has internal auditors develop recommendations that address a finding's root cause, and its considerations add that cost should be weighed against benefit. The cause is that the system allows two records for one supplier, so a rule blocking that fixes it at little cost. A second review of every payment, the closest choice, could also stop duplicates, but it treats the symptom and costs far more than the $3,000 at stake.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it could catch duplicates before payment, but it leaves the duplicate records in place and costs far more than the loss it prevents.
wrong_explanations.C: A recovery review finds duplicates after the money has left and leaves the cause untouched. An outside firm's fee may exceed $3,000.
wrong_explanations.D: Cleaning up the records is management's action. Internal audit recommends and later confirms; it does not carry out the fix.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a recovery review acts after payment and leaves the cause, and D, because carrying out the fix is management's job.
Final two: A beats B because blocking duplicate records removes the cause at little cost, while reviewing every payment treats the symptom at a cost above the loss.
Exam cue: for the BEST recommendation, pick the option aimed at the stated root cause whose cost is in proportion to the risk.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. Design gap or operating failure
questions.question: At a Mexican engineering firm, all 40 sampled expense claims carry the required supervisor approval, but the procedure sends supervisors no receipts to check. Which conclusion by internal auditor Diego Luna is MOST accurate?

options.A: The control is effective, as each sampled claim was approved
options.B: The control is well designed but is not being operated
options.C: The control would be effective if the sample were larger
options.D: The control operates as written, but its design is inadequate

questions.key_concept: Design asks whether a control would manage the risk if performed as written; operation asks whether it is performed that way.
questions.pre_read: Ask two questions in turn: is the control done as written, and could it work if done?
questions.correct_explanation: Design asks whether a control would manage the risk if performed as written; operation asks whether it is performed. Here supervisors approve every claim exactly as the procedure says, so operation is sound, but an approver who sees no receipts cannot catch a false claim: the design is inadequate. Standard 14.3's considerations treat design adequacy and effectiveness as separate judgments. Blaming the supervisors, the closest choice, misses that they followed the procedure.

wrong_explanations.A: Approval on every claim shows the step was performed. It does not show that an approval given without receipts can catch a false claim.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it separates design from operation but reverses them. Supervisors did what the procedure says; the procedure itself gives them nothing to check.
wrong_explanations.C: Sample size is not the problem. A larger sample would show more approvals made the same way, without receipts.

tips: Eliminate: A, because performing a step is different from managing the risk, and C, because more samples would repeat the same result.
Final two: D beats B because the supervisors followed the procedure exactly; the weakness is in what the procedure gives them to check.
Exam cue: when a control is performed every time yet could not catch the problem, the conclusion is a design weakness, not an operating failure.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. Effective but not efficient
questions.question: A Greek port checks every container document three times; no errors get through, trucks queue four hours, and tests show one check catches the same errors. Which is internal auditor Eleni Kosta's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The control is effective and efficient, so nothing needs reporting
options.B: The control is effective but inefficient, which merits reporting
options.C: The control is ineffective, since the delay harms the port
options.D: The control is effective, and efficiency is outside assurance work

questions.key_concept: Effective means the risk is managed; efficient means it is managed at a proportionate cost. They are separate tests.
questions.pre_read: Judge the control twice: does it manage the risk, and at what cost?
questions.correct_explanation: Effective means the risk is managed: no errors get through. Efficient means it is managed at a proportionate cost, and three checks with a four-hour queue fail that test when one check does the same job. Treating efficiency as outside assurance work is the closest choice, but Standard 9.1 lists efficient operations among the key risk areas, and Standard 14.2's considerations count efficiency improvements among potential findings.

wrong_explanations.A: Stopping every error makes the control effective. Two extra checks and a four-hour queue for the same result mean it is not efficient.
wrong_explanations.C: The control does manage its risk, since no errors get through. Delay is a cost of the control, which is an efficiency point.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the first half is right, but assurance covers efficiency as well, and chances to improve it can be reported as findings.

tips: Eliminate: A, because one check would do the same job at less cost, and C, because a control that stops every error is effective.
Final two: B beats D because potential findings include efficiency improvements, so an effective but wasteful control is worth reporting.
Exam cue: test a control twice, for whether it manages the risk and for what that costs; passing one test does not pass the other.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. What a control framework is for
questions.question: A finance head at a Rwandan city council says a recognized internal control framework was adopted last year, so internal audit can skip finance. How should internal auditor Jean Mugisha BEST regard the framework?

options.A: As a legal requirement that finance has now met
options.B: As evidence that finance's controls are adequately designed
options.C: As criteria for assessing whether finance's controls work
options.D: As management's tool, with no use in audit planning

questions.key_concept: An internal control framework gives a structure and criteria for assessing controls; adopting it does not show that the controls work.
questions.pre_read: Ask what adopting a framework changes on the day it is adopted.
questions.correct_explanation: A control framework describes what a sound system of internal control contains, so it works as a yardstick. Standard 13.2 requires internal auditors to gather applicable frameworks that can serve as criteria, and Standard 13.4's considerations list frameworks among adequate criteria. Adopting one says what finance is aiming for. It does not show that the controls built to meet it are well designed, which is why the closest choice fails, or that they operate.

wrong_explanations.A: A framework is guidance applied with judgment. It binds an organization only where a law or regulator says so, and adopting it does not prove that any rule is met.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: adoption shows which model finance aims at. Whether each control is adequately designed still has to be assessed against that model.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal auditors gather applicable frameworks during planning because they supply criteria. A framework management uses is directly relevant to the engagement.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a framework is guidance unless a law or regulator requires it, and D, because frameworks give internal auditors criteria during planning.
Final two: C beats B because adopting a model states an aim; design and operation of the controls still have to be assessed against it.
Exam cue: treat a framework as a yardstick; adopting one is never evidence that governance, risk management or controls work.
